docs.text: Evaluation of stabilizer codes under device noise, and search for codes, encoders, and syndrome-extraction schedules that score well under it.

docs.title: What is autoqec-sim?
docs.text:
autoqec-sim evaluates stabilizer codes and their circuits under device noise, and searches for codes, encoders, and syndrome-extraction schedules that score well under it.

The evaluation layer scores a code three ways: the undetected single-fault mass of its encoding circuit under a device noise profile with every parameter sourced, a multi-round memory experiment with a decoder, and the exact distance and weight enumerators that verify any claim independently of the objective. The search layer runs on a batched Aaronson-Gottesman tableau that holds thousands of encoding circuits as one array and advances them one Clifford gate per step on a chosen connectivity graph. PPO, with an optional lattice-equivariant policy, and an evolutionary search build encoders gate by gate; a schedule synthesizer assigns the CX layers of a fixed code's syndrome-extraction circuit against the exact circuit-level fault distance.

The gate-by-gate discovery mode follows 1, whose code, QDX, introduced it and has reached larger codes than this package has. autoqec-sim rediscovers [[5,1,3]], Steane, Shor, and the rotated surface code on every lattice tested and has found noise-adapted non-CSS codes up to 16 qubits, but no new code above that; Experiments records where it stops. Its schedule synthesizer raised the fault distance of the [[49,13,4]] circuit on the qldpc-challenge board from 2 to 3. For code design at larger sizes, the SAT formulation of 2 designs codes with up to 100 qubits; the evaluation and schedule tools here take such codes as input.

The numpy engine on the CPU is the reference. The same kernels and rewards run on CUDA through the torch backend, with two opt-in fused CUDA kernels for the gate updates and the parity masks.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
Install with pip install git+https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/autoqec-sim, then score three known codes under the IonQ Forte preset:

from autoqec_sim import known_codes
from autoqec_sim.memory_objective import MemoryObjective
from autoqec_sim.noise import presets

# A three-round memory experiment under the IonQ Forte preset at a quarter of
# its measured rates, scored by the low-weight maximum-likelihood proxy.
objective = MemoryObjective(presets.forte("sequential"), scale=0.25, rounds=3)
for name in ("five_qubit", "steane", "rotated_surface_9"):
    code = known_codes.get(name)
    print(name, code.parameters(), f"error per round {objective.evaluate(code).p_round:.2e}")

five_qubit (5, 1, 3) error per round 4.26e-03
steane (7, 1, 3) error per round 2.09e-03
rotated_surface_9 (9, 1, 3) error per round 5.89e-04

The Quick Start adds the search for a code, its verification against the reference, and the encoder score under a device profile.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Batched tableau simulator

    One (batch, 2n, 2n+1) array of Aaronson-Gottesman tableaux. Gates apply to selected batch elements with per-element qubit indices through gather and scatter indexing, with no Python loop over the batch, and are cross-checked against stim.

  • Rewards for code quality

    Knill-Laflamme undetected-error mass, exact distance, an LDPC sparsity constraint, circuit-level noise under sourced device presets, and a multi-round memory objective with a decoder.

  • Two agents and a regression

    PPO with action masking and a permutation-equivariant policy, and an evolutionary search. The rediscovery regression verifies each found code by exact distance and weight enumerators.

  • CPU reference, GPU backend

    The numpy engine is the reference. The torch backend runs the same kernels on CUDA with bit-for-bit agreement tests, and two fused CUDA kernels take the gate step and the parity masks further.

For a fixed code, autoqec-schedule trains a PPO policy on the exact circuit fault distance of the syndrome-extraction circuit and confirms the best CX-layer schedule at rounds = d. See Commands.

docs.title: What's New in 0.2.0
docs.text:
Release 0.2.0 is the first tagged release. On top of 0.1.0 it adds the noise module as the autoqec_sim.noise subpackage, with biased, correlated, and leakage-aware channels, device timing, topologies, and sourced presets for IonQ Forte, a long ion chain, IBM Heron, and the qldpc-challenge recipe. The circuit-level reward lays each gate list out as a TICK-layered skeleton so a profile's timing and idle model apply, and cross-checks its result against stim's detector error model.

The LDPC constraint computes the exact minimum bottleneck generator weight per batch element and enters the environment as a hard constraint or a reward penalty. The PPO agent matches the evolutionary search on every rediscovery target with 3 to 17 times fewer state evaluations, and the memory objective scores a multi-round syndrome-extraction circuit with three fidelity tiers. The torch backend and two fused CUDA kernels run the reward engine on a GPU.

Full Changelog

  1. Jan Olle, Remmy Zen, Matteo Puviani, and Florian Marquardt. Simultaneous discovery of quantum error correction codes and encoders with a noise-aware reinforcement learning agent. npj Quantum Information, 10:126, 2024. arXiv:2311.04750, doi:10.1038/s41534-024-00920-y. ↩

  2. Ben DalFavero, William M. Watkins, Margarite L. LaBorde, Vincent Russo, Ethan Egger, Gregory Quiroz, and Ryan LaRose. Satisfying quantum codes: Physics-informed and hardware-aware code design with SAT solvers. 2026. arXiv:2608.23460. ↩

docs.title: Noise-aware discovery
docs.text:
experiments/noise_aware.py asks whether the code PPO discovers depends on the noise profile it is trained against, and in the direction the profile's structure predicts (the experiment the proposal cites 1 for). Three autoqec_sim.noise profiles scaled to the same total fault mass (board depolarizing; Forte 2 ion chain with sequential timing, so idle dephasing dominates; Heron r2 rates 3 on the setting's graph), three settings (7 qubits all-to-all with H, S, CNOT and target distance 3; 3x3 lattice with H, CNOT and distance 3; 4x4 lattice with H, CNOT and distance 4), five PPO seeds per cell. The reward is the shifted distance reward plus, on states at the target distance, the circuit-level undetected fault mass (normalize=False) and the LDPC penalty at w_max = 4; the exact combination, the calibration, the cross-evaluation matrices, the code lists, the known-code baselines, and the verdict are in experiments/noise_aware/runs/REPORT.md. One cell reproduces with

uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.noise_aware run --setting 3x3 --profile ion --seed 0
uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.noise_aware baselines --setting 3x3
uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.noise_aware report

(--threads N caps torch and BLAS; experiments/noise_aware/runs/run_sweep.sh with the job scripts under experiments/noise_aware/runs/jobs/ is the 3-worker, 6-thread queue the release numbers came from.)

Result (45 runs, 15 per setting): the discovered code depends strongly on the training profile, but through the encoding circuit's fault propagation rather than through X/Z structure. Board-trained codes have 3.4x less undetected fault mass on the board profile than ion- or heron-trained codes (25 of 25 seed pairs, permutation p = 0.008, both settings) and ion-trained codes 1.3x to 1.6x less on the ion profile (p = 0.008 and 0.048); ion- and heron-trained codes are interchangeable at n = 7. No profile produced codes with d_Z > d_X more often than another (0/5 or 1/5 seeds everywhere), none of the 30 codes is CSS or local-Clifford equivalent to a CSS code, and the mechanism breakdown shows the board-trained circuits detect every idle fault while ion-trained circuits leave idle X and Y faults undetected, faults the ion profile hardly emits. The discovered degenerate codes beat Steane 4 (n = 7) and the rotated surface code and its XZZX 5 and Hadamard-deformed variants (3x3) with polished encoders under every profile; a Hadamard deformation of the code is invisible to this single-fault circuit objective, which is one reason no such structure emerges. The 4x4 setting (target d = 4) did not fit the budget: none of its 15 runs (16M steps each) produced a distance-4 state, with either the level or the fractional distance term. Without the padding penalty the agent embeds a smaller code and leaves qubits idle.

docs.title: Memory objective
docs.text:
memory_objective.py scores a code by the logical error rate per round of an R-round syndrome-extraction memory experiment instead of by its encoder's single-fault mass, which cannot see a local-Clifford deformation of the code (a Hadamard at the end of the encoder relabels weight-1 faults, all detected; experiments/noise_aware/runs/REPORT.md). The circuit is built for arbitrary (non-CSS) generators, one ancilla per generator with controlled-X/Y/Z gates in a hook-aware order (hook_orders: without it the sorted order gives the Shor code a circuit-level distance of 1 in the Z basis), generators that share a qubit with different Pauli letters in separate batches so every interleaving commutes (X block then Z block for a CSS code), optional one-flag ancillas, noiseless MPP preparation and readout, and an all-to-all or square:RxC layout (ancilla sites at the plaquette centers, non-local generators routed with CNOT ladders and run in their own batch). The noise is a autoqec_sim.noise.Profile with its timing model; stim's detector error model feeds three tiers:

tier what cost per code, both bases, R = d, one thread proxy leading-order failure of the maximum-likelihood decoder over fault sets of weight at most two, plus exact d_circ up to weight 4 (exact_dcirc, from ion-search/lib.py) 0.08 to 0.22 s at n <= 9 (the DEM derivation dominates), 1.7 to 2.3 s for the [[16,4,4]] code (about 2000 mechanisms, 60 detectors) sampled exact ML decoder by dynamic program when detectors plus observables <= 20 (no shots), else a weight-2 lookup decoder with a one-mechanism completion, sampled 0.16 to 0.31 s at n <= 9 (5000 shots grown to 200 failures), 5 s at n = 16 bposd the board's pinned BP+OSD 67 (ldpc, uv run --with ldpc), sampled; validation only 0.2 to 1.5 s at n <= 9, 37 to 42 s at n = 16

MemoryReward(objective, d*) is the environment reward: the distance and padding terms of the noise-aware experiment plus 0.1 * log10(p_ref / p_round) on target-distance states (cached per code); CodeDiscoveryEnv adopts its success_fn. Design note: docs/memory_objective.md; runs: experiments/memory_objective/REPORT.md (python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.memory_objective {benchmark,random,random-check,bias,lattice,ppo,report}).

Results (chain preset at scale 0.25, board at 1, Heron at 0.1; the tiers are leading-order or sampled estimates and need the expected number of faults per shot below about one, which the presets at scale 1 exceed):

  • Rank agreement. On 32 random [[9,1,3]] codes (R = 3) the Spearman correlation of the proxy against bposd is 0.79 (ion), 0.90 (board), 0.78 (heron); on the five benchmark codes 0.9, 0.8, 0.3, where the outlier is Steane, for which bposd is 1.7 to 3.2 times worse than both the proxy and the near-ML lookup decoder (proxy against lookup 0.9 on every profile). The proxy is within 25 percent of the exact-ML or lookup sampled tier on every benchmark code below one expected fault per shot; bposd deviates where it decodes badly (Steane, the [[16,4,4]] code under the ion preset at 2x).
  • Bias sensitivity. Rotated surface against XZZX at n = 9, R = 3, every rate 2.5e-4 with a slot idle channel of bias eta: the ratio p_round(plain) / p_round(xzzx) is 1.00 at eta = 0.5 (exact tie, the deformation is a relabeling), 1.21 at 2, 1.80 at 10, 2.27 at pure Z under sequential timing (bposd 1.08, 1.23, 1.89, 2.19), and 1.00 to 2.10 under parallel timing. Under the Forte set (duration idle, eta = 10) the proxy prefers XZZX by 1.22 and the lookup decoder by 1.21; bposd does not (0.78). Under the chain set the two tie (0.99): its idle is small and its readout flips dominate.
  • Flags. One flag per generator lifts d_circ from 2 to 3 for [[5,1,3]], Steane, the [[16,4,4]] code, and the non-CSS 3x3 code, and lowers the ion p_round by 2.6 to 4.4 times (0.23 to 0.38 of the bare value); on the board recipe the extra gates cost more than the flags gain (1.0 to 1.5 times the bare value).
  • Lattice. On square:3x3 the surface and XZZX codes route nothing; the non-CSS 3x3 code needs 63 extra two-qubit gates per round (270 against 81 in 3 rounds) and 7 sequential batches, and its board p_round goes from 0.018 to 0.26.
  • PPO smoke run (3x3 lattice, H and CNOT, chain profile at 0.25, R = 3, batch 256, 400k env steps, 62 s at one thread): distance 3 reached at 83k env steps, 92 distinct target-distance codes evaluated at 0.47 s each (44 s of memory evaluation in total, all-to-all layout); the best has p_round 0.0016 against 0.00077 for the rotated surface code. The test-suite version (R = 2, 300k steps) is the regression.

docs.title: RL scaling probe
docs.text:
experiments/scaling.py asks how far the PPO agent scales in n and what the cheapest change is that gets it to a distance-4 code on the 4x4 lattice (the setting the noise-aware experiment could not solve), plus how the LDPC-constrained target behaves at n = 12 to 16. Findings, from experiments/scaling/REPORT.md: the 4x4 failure is exploration (d = 4 states within 50 gates exist but are too rare for the default policy to ever see one). This holds for this setting, nearest-neighbor 4x4 connectivity, the unrestricted H and CNOT action space, and 50-gate episodes; a flat policy with CSS-restricted actions on a next-to-nearest-neighbor periodic lattice reaches distance 5 at 17 qubits in 1. Here a per-qubit permutation-equivariant policy (now agents.policies.equivariant_actor_critic, PPOConfig(policy="equivariant")) reaches a clean [[16, 1, 4]] at the 50-gate cap in 0.2M to 0.26M env steps on every seed (about 20x fewer than the flat MLP with a 4x larger batch, which also works), and it is the recommended default for n >= 12. The LDPC penalty form of the regression does not carry over: in 18 runs at n = 12 to 16 no PPO policy reached a distance-3 code with w* <= 4; all converge to sparse groups of distance 1, so the penalty is validated at n = 9 only. The limits above are limits of gate-by-gate encoder search. Code design under hardware constraints is NP-complete in general, and a SAT formulation nonetheless designs physics-inspired codes with up to 100 physical qubits in minutes and hardware-aware codes for biased noise with lower logical error rates than surface codes 8; that search space, check matrices rather than encoding circuits, is where the rewards here (circuit-level noise, the memory objective) and the schedule synthesizer take a code as input. One run reproduces with

uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.scaling variant --variant equivariant --seed 0
uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.scaling ldpc --n 12 --k 2 --graph all_to_all:12 --seed 0
uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.scaling report

docs.title: Three-topology run matrix
docs.text:
experiments/topologies.py runs the PPO agent by itself (not the LLM meta-agent) on square, triangular, and heavy-hex lattices with one objective and one metric set: a [[n, 1, d >= 3]] code with no idle qubit, H and CNOT on the lattice edges, 50-gate episodes, the level distance reward of the scaling probe, PPOConfig defaults with policy="auto", three seeds per cell. Two tiers: 3x3 and 4x4 for square and triangular (n = 9, 16); heavy-hex takes the nearest sizes the honeycomb construction allows, 1x1 (n = 12, a 12-cycle) and 2x1 (n = 18). Every cell reports success, env steps and wall time to first success, the best code (exact d, w*, maximum qubit degree, CSS test, weight enumerators), the undetected fault mass of its encoder under the Heron preset on the cell's graph and under the board preset, and the same mass for the rotated surface encoder routed onto the graph where one exists. Results and the write-up are in experiments/topologies/runs/REPORT.md: all 18 runs reached distance 3, at 6k to 12k env steps on the 9-qubit lattices (within the first three updates, before any learning), 49k to 113k at 12 and 16 qubits, and 307k to 345k on the 18-qubit heavy-hex graph.

uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.topologies matrix
uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.topologies run --topology heavy_hex --target-n 16 --seed 0
uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.topologies report

docs.title: Evolutionary search against PPO
docs.text:
autoqec_sim.experiments.topologies_ea runs the three-topology matrix with the package's evolutionary search in place of the PPO agent: same cells, objective ([[n, 1, 3]] with no idle qubit), gate set, 50-gate episodes, and environment-step budget per tier (evolutionary evaluations count as whole episodes). Run 16 October 2026 on one laptop; results in experiments/topologies_ea/runs/.

lattice n PPO successes PPO median steps to success EA successes EA median steps to success EA median wall square 9 3/3 9,472 0/3 none 22 s triangular 9 3/3 7,424 0/3 none 24 s heavy_hex 12 3/3 63,488 0/3 none 21 s square 16 3/3 112,128 0/3 none 54 s triangular 16 3/3 75,776 0/3 none 46 s heavy_hex 18 3/3 340,480 0/3 none 38 s

Totals: PPO 18 of 18 runs succeed, evolutionary search 0 of 18. The evolutionary search is autoqec-sim's own (population of gate sequences, mutation, one batched rollout per generation), not a tuned evolutionary agent; the comparison fixes the budget, objective, and action space, nothing else.

docs.title: QDX's targets
docs.text:
autoqec_sim.experiments.qdx_targets runs the full target set that QDX, the code of 1, publishes for all-to-all connectivity at n <= 15 (50 [[n, k, d]] triples with d up to 5) through this package's PPO at matched gate set, connectivity, and success criterion, one run per target with a budget of 3M environment steps or 10 minutes, and verifies each result by exact distance. experiments/qdx_targets/REPORT.md holds the table; the QDX columns are read from its archive of discovered codes.

uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.qdx_targets run --tier d3
uv run --extra rl python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.qdx_targets report

docs.title: SAT-designed codes under the memory objective
docs.text:
autoqec_sim.experiments.sat_codes takes the 9-qubit surface-like codes that 8 sampled by SAT and ranked by exact maximum-likelihood logical error rate under code-capacity biased noise, selects the twelve best distinct codes at bias 10 and three of the worst, and scores them with the circuit-level memory objective against the rotated surface code and its XZZX deformation under a biased idle profile at three bias values and under the Forte preset, at the proxy and sampled tiers. The question is whether the code-capacity ranking survives circuit-level noise. experiments/sat_codes/REPORT.md holds the tables and the rank correlations.

uv run python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.sat_codes run
uv run python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.sat_codes report

docs.title: A population of SAT-designed codes
docs.text:
autoqec_sim.experiments.sat_population scales the previous experiment from fifteen codes to a population: a uniform random sample of 2,000 of the 43,563 distinct stabilizer groups among the 100,000 codes of 8, plus the 100 best and the 50 worst by the source's code-capacity rate at bias 10, scored under four cases (biased idle at source bias 4 and 10, every channel biased at bias 10, and the Forte preset) at the proxy and sampled tiers. The report gives the rank correlation between the two scores, the overlap of their best sets, the circuit-level rates of the source's best codes against random ones, the structural features of a code's extraction circuit that predict its circuit-level rate, and the best codes of the population against the rotated surface code and XZZX. experiments/sat_population/REPORT.md holds the tables and the figure. The prepare step reads the source repository's experiments/surface/ directory and writes experiments/sat_population/population.json, which is committed.

Findings, from the report. Where a case is named Forte, it is the package's Forte preset, a noise model assembled from public specifications, not a measurement on a device. The 100,000 sampled codes contain 62,876 distinct generator lists but 43,563 distinct stabilizer groups. The source's code-capacity rate at bias 10 has Spearman 0.09 to 0.21 with the circuit-level rate under the biased cases and 0.00 under Forte, and none of the 20 best codes by one score is among the 20 best by the other in any case. The 100 codes the source ranks best score worse than the random sample under bias (median 0.00063 against 0.00051 at bias 10, sampled tier) and no better under Forte. Every code in the sample has exactly 24 weight-3 logical operators, so at code capacity under depolarizing noise they are identical to leading order, while their circuit-level rates under Forte span a factor of 2.6; the spread is in how many space-time realizations of those logicals go undetected in the extraction circuit (342 weight-3 undetectable fault sets for the best codes against 462 to 472 for the worst, a tenfold spread in probability mass). The mass of those fault sets over both memory bases, a quantity only a circuit-level evaluator computes, predicts the rate in every case (Spearman 0.70 to 0.73, R^2 0.47 to 0.61 for a log-log fit), and under bias the low-rate weight-3 mass computed from the stabilizers alone predicts better than the source's exact maximum-likelihood rate at its working point of 1e-2. Confirmed at three percent standard error, the best codes of the population sit 30 to 40 percent below XZZX under Forte and under both bias-10 cases (0.00034 against 0.00049 under Forte); about half the random sample beats XZZX under Forte and two thirds beat the rotated surface code.

experiments/sat_population/local_search.py is a prototype of the design loop these numbers argue for: SAT keeps every candidate a valid distance-3 code on the footprint, CMSGen samples completions with all but two generators fixed, and the Forte proxy tier ranks them. Three runs of 40 steps reached proxy rates of 0.000331 to 0.000365 in 129 to 159 evaluations, against 0.000344 for the best of the 2,000 random draws and 0.000351 for the median best of 150 draws. At the sampled tier the best search result and the population's best code are 0.000333 and 0.000337, so the search reaches the random-sampling floor in about a fifteenth of the evaluations and does not pass it; on this footprint the floor appears to be structural. The script needs the source repository's qodesign package, pycmsgen, and python-sat.

uv run python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.sat_population prepare --source <satisfying-codes>/experiments/surface
uv run python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.sat_population run --workers 4
uv run python -m autoqec_sim.experiments.sat_population report

docs.title: The torch backend on a GPU
docs.text: autoqec_sim.backends.torch_backend runs the two hot paths of the reward engine (the tableau gate kernels and the parity masks behind every reward) on torch tensors on cpu or cuda. This page says what it covers, how to measure it on a RunPod GPU with benchmarks/profile_tableau.py, and what is still specific to cuQuantum. The GPU table was measured on a RunPod A40 on 2026-09-21.

docs.title: What the backend covers
docs.text:
Same array layout as numpy: (batch, 2n, 2n + 1) uint8, so torch_backend.from_numpy(tab, device) and torch_backend.to_numpy(t) move a state between the backends without conversion. Functions have the names and semantics of their numpy counterparts in tableau, symplectic, and reward:

  • gate kernels apply_h, apply_s, apply_s_dag, apply_x, apply_y, apply_z, apply_cnot, apply_cz, apply_swap, apply_gate, and ActionTable(table_or_entries, device) with the three lookup arrays on the device and apply(tab, actions) grouped by gate type;
  • symplectic_product, swap_halves, code_rows;
  • undetected_mask, in_stabilizer_mask, batched_distance, kl_reward, distance_reward, low_weight_stabilizer_penalty, CompositeReward, make_kl_reward(errors, device=...), make_low_weight_penalty, make_distance_reward;
  • numpy_reward_adapter(fn, device): a torch reward as a reward_fn for CodeDiscoveryEnv (the environment itself stays numpy; the tableau is copied to the device once per step and the (batch,) result back).

Parity test. The numpy path computes the float32 product of the error set against the n + k code rows, casts it to int64, masks the low bit, and runs two boolean any() reductions; on the CPU the cast and the reductions are about 80 percent of the reward (docs/profile.md). The torch path reduces the product mod 2 in place in float32 (remainder_(2), exact since the entries are integers below 2n) and decides both tests with one matrix-vector product against a weight vector: stabilizer columns weigh 2k + 1, logical columns 1, so the score of an error is s (2k + 1) + l with s anticommuting stabilizers and l anticommuting logicals, and the error is undetected iff 1 <= score <= 2k. The peak intermediate is one float32 (batch, chunk, n + k) block, 4 M (n + k) bytes per element instead of 12 M (n + k), and no boolean (batch, chunk, n + k) array exists. tests/test_torch_backend.py checks every kernel and every mask against numpy bit for bit at n in 5, 9, 16 on random tableaux and on the known codes.

docs.title: CPU torch against numpy (measured)
docs.text:
Same machine and setting as docs/profile.md (Apple M5 Pro, six BLAS threads, torch 2.14.0 CPU, all-to-all graph, gates H, S, CNOT, k = 1, Knill-Laflamme reward over all Paulis of weight 1 and 2 plus the weight-1 penalty, batch 1024, 2026-09-21):

n backend reward intermediate B/elem gate applications/s reward evaluations/s env steps/s 9 numpy 41.1 KiB 6.51 M 83.8 k 94.2 k 9 torch cpu 13.7 KiB 3.08 M 155.8 k 147.3 k 16 numpy 224.7 KiB 4.84 M 23.3 k 28.0 k 16 torch cpu 74.9 KiB 2.82 M 54.2 k 53.0 k 25 numpy 845.5 KiB 3.57 M 10.7 k 11.4 k 25 torch cpu 281.8 KiB 2.04 M 21.4 k 21.2 k

The reward is 1.9 (n = 9) to 2.3 (n = 16) times faster on CPU torch; the gate kernels are about half the numpy rate (torch advanced-indexing overhead on small tensors) and are one to two percent of an environment step, so the env-steps column follows the reward. Breakdown at n = 16, batch 1024, torch cpu: GEMM 5.95 ms, remainder_(2) 5.15 ms, score GEMV and compares 3.02 ms, against 5.81, 10.00, and 19.94 ms for the numpy GEMM, int64 cast, and two reductions. The n = 25 numpy row is from docs/profile.md.

docs.title: Running the profile on a RunPod pod
docs.text:
The pod image has torch 2.8.0+cu128 with CUDA available. One point about the install: the package's rl extra pins torch>=2.14.0 and, on Linux, resolves torch from the CPU-only PyTorch index, so uv sync --extra rl or pip install -e .[rl] would replace the pod's CUDA torch with a CPU one. Install without the extra into the pod's Python and keep its torch:

# on the laptop: the repository, without build and result directories

# the profile: numpy on the pod's CPU, torch on its CPU, torch on the GPU
python benchmarks/profile_tableau.py --backend numpy --json pod_numpy.json
python benchmarks/profile_tableau.py --backend torch --device cpu --json pod_torch_cpu.json
python benchmarks/profile_tableau.py --backend torch --device cuda --mem-cap-gb 16 --json pod_torch_cuda.json

--mem-cap-gb should stay below the GPU's memory: the reward intermediate is 4 M (n + k) bytes per batch element (2.0 GiB at n = 49, batch 1024; 8.1 GiB at batch 4096), and undetected_mask(..., chunk=...) bounds it by chunking the error set if a cell has to run under a tighter cap. Timing synchronizes the device after every call (torch.cuda.synchronize), so the rates include kernel launch and, in the env-steps column, the host-to-device copy of the tableau per step. docs.title: GPU result (RunPod A40, 2026-09-21)
docs.text:
Measured on a dedicated RunPod pod: NVIDIA A40 (44 GiB, CUDA 12.8), torch 2.8.0+cu128, Python 3.12.3, numpy 2.1.2 (scipy-openblas), GPU idle before the run (0 percent, 0 MiB). The host's CPUs were shared with other tenants (load average 15 on 96 visible cores), so the pod numpy column is slowed and the laptop numpy column (docs/profile.md, Apple M5 Pro, 6 threads, unloaded) is the fair CPU reference. Raw records: experiments/profile_pod/runs/torch_cuda_clean.json and experiments/profile_pod/runs/numpy_pod3.json; an earlier run on a pod whose GPU was already at 100 percent from another job (torch_cuda.json, numpy_pod.json) gave 4 to 5 times lower GPU rates and is kept as the contended reference. Render any of them with python benchmarks/profile_tableau.py --render experiments/profile_pod/runs/<file>.json.

Reward evaluations per second (the term that is 99 percent of an env step on the CPU):

n batch torch cuda (A40) numpy, pod CPU (shared host) numpy, laptop GPU / laptop 5 4096 5.77 M 102.5 k 197.7 k 29x 9 4096 2.40 M 23.8 k 79.9 k 30x 16 1024 674.0 k 6.0 k 24.4 k 28x 16 4096 798.4 k 5.5 k 24.4 k 33x 25 1024 228.2 k 2.1 k 10.7 k 21x 25 4096 240.4 k 2.0 k 10.6 k 23x 49 256 36.4 k not run 1.7 k 21x 49 1024 37.8 k not run (6.1 GiB) not run (6.1 GiB)

Gate applications per second on the GPU: 244 k to 282 k at batch 256, 1.1 M at 1024, 3.5 M to 4.5 M at 4096, independent of n (launch-bound: one nonzero per gate type per call). The numpy kernels run at 1 M to 8 M on the laptop, so gates are at parity at batch 4096 and slower at small batches; on the CPU they are 1 to 2 percent of a step, on the GPU 10 to 40 percent of the hybrid env steps/s column (512.5 k at n = 16, batch 4096, against 798.4 k reward evaluations). A fused per-element gate kernel is the first cuQuantum-specific item below.

The (B, M, n+k) intermediate at n = 49, batch 1024 is 2.0 GiB on the torch path (float32, in place) against 6.1 GiB on the numpy path, which is why the GPU runs that cell and the CPU paths do not; at batch 4096 (8.2 GiB) the profile's 4 GiB cap stops both. The GPU reward rate keeps rising with the batch at every n up to 16 (n = 16: 358.7 k, 674.0 k, 798.4 k at 256, 1024, 4096) and is flat from 1024 at n = 25 and 49, where the GEMM itself saturates the device.

The whole torch run took 20 s and the reduced numpy run 60 s.

docs.title: Done here versus cuQuantum-specific
docs.text:
Done in the torch backend (items 1 to 3 of the README's "What is left for cuQuantum" list, on any torch device):

  • the gate kernels and ActionTable as gather/scatter operations on device tensors;
  • code_rows as a device-side slice and concatenation;
  • the symplectic product and the parity masks with the mod-2 reduction in place and both commutation tests as one GEMV, a third of the numpy intermediate and none of its int64 or boolean copies;
  • the profile with --backend, --device, --json, --render.

Still specific to cuQuantum (cuStabilizer) or to a custom CUDA kernel:

  • the bit-packed popcount product with parity, the stabilizer test, and the logical test fused in one pass, which removes the GEMM and the (batch, chunk, n + k) intermediate altogether; torch has no batched popcount matmul, so the torch path keeps a float32 block per chunk;
  • a fused per-element gate kernel: ActionTable.apply groups actions by gate type with one nonzero per type, each a host synchronization on cuda; a kernel that reads the gate id per batch element needs no grouping;
  • the environment on the device: CodeDiscoveryEnv is numpy (history, masks, auto-reset), so the torch reward is reached through numpy_reward_adapter and the tableau crosses the PCIe bus once per step (1 KiB per element at n = 16, 9.5 KiB at n = 49);
  • integration with the PPO agent's tensors (the observation encoder reads the numpy tableau; a device-resident environment would hand the policy the tableau bits without a copy).

Not on the hot path and left on the host as before: GF(2) elimination, exact distance and enumerators in code, stim conversion, the circuit-level fault propagation, and the search agent's population update.

docs.title: What is left for cuQuantum
docs.text:
The state is one array tab of shape (batch, 2n, 2n+1) with dtype uint8. Everything a GPU backend has to provide:

  1. Gate kernels (tableau.apply_h, apply_s, apply_s_dag, apply_cnot, apply_cz, apply_swap, apply_x/y/z): each reads two or four columns of the selected batch elements (tab[b, :, q], a gather along axis 2 with a per-element column index) and writes them back after elementwise XOR/AND. ActionTable.apply groups a vector of actions by gate type and calls these once per type; with a fused kernel the grouping disappears.
  2. The symplectic product symplectic.symplectic_product(E, rows): a batched GEMM of the shared error set (M, 2n) against the per-element code rows (batch, n+k, 2n) followed by a parity reduction. This is the whole cost of reward.undetected_mask, in_stabilizer_mask, batched_distance, and hence of every reward. Bit-packed rows and a popcount-based product would replace float32.
  3. reward.code_rows: a slice-and-concatenate of the tableau; on device it is a view.

Not on the hot path and fine to leave on the host: GF(2) elimination in symplectic, exact distance and enumerators in code, stim conversion, the circuit-level fault propagation (per circuit, uses stim), and the search agent's population update.

Measured on the CPU (benchmarks/profile_tableau.py, docs/profile.md; numpy on one laptop, not a GPU): the reward is 99% of an environment step at n = 16, batch 1024, and the gate kernels 1%, at every n from 5 to 49. Inside the reward the float32 GEMM of item 2 is about 15% of the Knill-Laflamme term; the int64 cast for the mod-2 reduction is about 30% and the two boolean any() reductions over the (batch, M, n + k) product more than half. So item 2 is the hot path, but a port that replaces the GEMM alone and keeps the cast and the reductions on the host gains little; the kernel to write is the fused bit-packed popcount product with the parity, the stabilizer-commutation test, and the logical-anticommutation test in one pass, which also removes the (batch, M, n + k) intermediate (0.8 MiB per batch element at n = 25, 6 MiB at n = 49, against 2.5 and 9.5 KiB for the tableau). Throughput on the CPU at batch 1024: 7.9 M gate applications per second and 204 k reward evaluations per second at n = 5, 4.8 M and 23 k at n = 16, 3.6 M and 11 k at n = 25.

The torch backend (autoqec_sim.backends.torch_backend, docs/gpu.md) is the interim version of items 1 to 3 on any torch device: the gate kernels and ActionTable as the same gather/scatter operations on torch tensors, and the parity test as a float32 GEMM reduced mod 2 in place plus one matrix-vector product that decides the stabilizer-commutation and logical-anticommutation tests together (stabilizer columns weigh 2k + 1, logical columns 1; undetected iff 1 <= score <= 2k). It removes the int64 copy and the two boolean reductions, and the intermediate is one float32 (batch, chunk, n + k) block, 4 M (n + k) bytes per element instead of 12 M (n + k). On CPU torch it is 1.9 to 2.3 times faster than numpy on the reward at n = 9 and 16 (batch 1024; the gate kernels run at half the numpy rate and are one to two percent of a step). benchmarks/profile_tableau.py --backend torch --device cuda --json produces the same table on a GPU; docs/gpu.md has the RunPod procedure and the A40 measurement of 2026-09-21 (798 k reward evaluations per second at n = 16, batch 4096, 33 times the laptop numpy rate; 240 k at n = 25, 23 times). What remains cuQuantum-specific after this is the bit-packed popcount kernel with parity and both tests fused, which removes the GEMM and the intermediate entirely, and a fused per-element gate kernel that avoids the per-gate-type nonzero synchronizations.

docs.title: Fused CUDA kernels
docs.text:
autoqec_sim.backends.cuda_kernels holds the two kernels the list above names, written as plain CUDA and compiled at first use through CuPy's NVRTC path (no nvcc, no toolkit beyond the driver):

  • apply_actions: one launch applies a per-element gate (any of the nine gates, per-element qubit indices) to every row of every selected tableau.
  • parity_codes: bit-packed popcount symplectic products of the error set against the code rows, reduced in the kernel to detected, undetected, or in-stabilizer per (element, error).

They are opt-in: AUTOQEC_CUDA_KERNELS=1 or cuda_kernels.enable(). The torch backend's agreement tests pass with them on, and tests/test_cuda_kernels.py compares them with the torch path directly. Measured on one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB (torch 2.8.0+cu129, benchmarks/bench_cuda_kernels.py, docs/data/bench_cuda_kernels_a100.json):

n batch errors gate step, torch path gate step, kernel undetected mask, torch path undetected mask, kernel 5 1024 105 2415 us 491 us (4.9x) 0.24 ms 0.39 ms (0.6x) 9 1024 351 2454 us 483 us (5.1x) 0.25 ms 0.38 ms (0.7x) 16 1024 1,128 2435 us 486 us (5.0x) 0.90 ms 0.38 ms (2.4x) 16 4096 1,128 2437 us 485 us (5.0x) 3.49 ms 0.41 ms (8.5x) 25 1024 2,775 2414 us 503 us (4.8x) 3.18 ms 0.40 ms (8.0x) 25 1024 64,875 2566 us 485 us (5.3x) 72.33 ms 5.59 ms (12.9x)

The parity kernel loses at a few hundred errors, where both paths are launch-bound, and wins by 8 to 13 times once the error set has thousands of rows, which is the regime of the Knill-Laflamme reward on 16 to 25 qubits.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: A discovery run fixes four things: the search space, the reward, the agent, and where the kernels run. The pages in this section cover each one.

docs.title: 1. Define the search space
docs.text: CodeDiscoveryEnv(n, k, graph, batch_size, reward_fn, gates, max_steps, seed) holds batch_size encoding circuits on n qubits as one array of stabilizer tableaux of shape (batch, 2n, 2n+1). Actions are single-qubit gates on every qubit and two-qubit gates on the edges of a connectivity graph from autoqec_sim.graphs (all-to-all, chain, square, triangular, heavy-hex 1, or a kind:size spec). Every builder delegates to autoqec_sim.noise.topology, so the action space and a noise profile's placement check share one edge set. Observations are the tableau bits, the (n-k) x 2n check matrix, or a flat vector. With auto_reset=True, finished episodes restart per element while the rest of the batch runs on.

docs.title: 2. Choose the reward
docs.text:
Reward Page Knill-Laflamme undetected mass 2 and exact distance, the default of the regression targets Rediscovery regression LDPC sparsity, as a hard constraint (terminate, mask, final) or a penalty LDPC constraint Circuit-level noise of the encoding circuit under a device profile Noise interface, Device presets Multi-round memory experiment with a decoder, three fidelity tiers Memory objective

regress.make_reward(target) composes the Knill-Laflamme term with the low-weight-stabilizer penalty and, on LDPC targets, the sparsity term. Any callable from the batched tableau to a reward vector works as reward_fn.

docs.title: 3. Choose the agent
docs.text:
search.EvolutionarySearch runs one batched rollout per generation on numpy alone. agents.ppo is a clipped PPO 3 with GAE 4, a shared value head, an entropy bonus, and action masking, on torch; agents.policies holds the flat MLP and the permutation-equivariant actor-critic. regress and agents.ppo_regress wrap both agents in the rediscovery regression, which verifies every distinct code a run produces by exact distance and weight enumerators.

Experiments records the noise-aware discovery runs, the memory-objective runs, the RL scaling probe, and the three-topology run matrix, with what each found and where the agent stops.

docs.title: 4. Choose where the kernels run
docs.text: The numpy engine on the CPU is the reference; CPU profile gives its throughput and where an environment step spends its time. The torch backend runs the gate kernels, the parity masks, and the rewards on cpu or cuda tensors with the same names and bit-for-bit agreement tests, and two opt-in fused CUDA kernels replace the gate step and the parity reduction.

docs.text:

docs.title: LDPC constraint
docs.text:
ldpc.sparsest_basis_stats computes, for each batch element, the exact minimum bottleneck generator weight w* (the smallest w such that the stabilizer elements of weight at most w generate the group; the optimal generator weight of 1, who show computing it is NP-hard in general) and the maximum qubit degree of a sparsest basis, by bit-packed GF(2) elimination over the enumerated group for n - k <= 14 (about 4 ms at n = 9), with a greedy pairwise reduction as the bound for larger codes. The environment takes ldpc_w_max with three modes: terminate (episode ends on a violating state with ldpc_violation_reward), mask (the violating action reverts to a no-op; feasible_action_mask() gives agents the mask to apply to logits), and final (only success is gated). ldpc_penalty is the soft form for the reward. w_max = 3 provably excludes every 5-qubit distance-3 code and empirically every 7-qubit one the search reaches; w_max = 4 admits [[5,1,3]] 2 and Steane 3 and excludes Shor's code 4 (w* = 6).

Above n = 9 the penalty form fails (experiments/scaling/REPORT.md): the normalized Knill-Laflamme 5 term pays 1/630 to 1/1128 per detected error against 0.25 per unit of w* excess, and PPO converges to sparse groups of distance 1. ldpc.LdpcObjective(n, k, d, w_max, form=...) is the reward and success criterion of an LDPC-constrained target in one of four forms (ldpc.LDPC_FORMS), all built from the same base terms (Knill-Laflamme term over the Paulis of weight below d, padding penalty) with the exact w* evaluated only on candidate states (every error detected, no idle qubit) and the greedy bound elsewhere:

form reward on every state success penalty normalized base minus scale * excess (the regression's form) reward 0 unnormalized one unit per undetected error and per weight-1 stabilizer, minus scale * excess, the sum divided by the initial state's undetected count; one undetected error costs 1 / scale units of w* excess reward 0 final the normalized base alone (hard final-state constraint) candidate with exact w* <= w_max schedule the normalized base until activate(), then the penalty form (the trainer switches once the success rate at the target distance reaches a threshold) any candidate before the switch, reward 0 after

regress.LdpcSpec(w_max, mode="objective", form=...) puts one of them on a regression target (make_reward returns the objective, env_kwargs hands its success method to the environment as success_fn); the n <= 9 targets keep mode="penalty". experiments.ldpc_scaling compares the forms on [[12, 2, 3]] and [[16, 4, 3]] with w_max = 4 on the all-to-all and the square graph, three seeds each, equivariant policy, 1.5M env steps or 20 minutes per run (experiments/ldpc_scaling/REPORT.md, runs in experiments/ldpc_scaling/runs/). Result (36 runs plus 4 scale variants, 0.62M to 1.5M env steps each on a shared machine): the unnormalized form is the default (ldpc.DEFAULT_LDPC_FORM). It learns distance where the penalty form never did (61 to 69 percent of terminal states at distance 3 on five of six [[12, 2, 3]] runs, 64 percent on the best 4x4-lattice seed) and it is the only form that produced codes within the bound: 3 of 12 runs, all [[12, 2, 3]] (303k and 354k env steps all-to-all, 950k on the lattice, 23 to 31 gates, w* = 4), each a single episode after which the policy keeps producing distance-3 codes with w* 5 to 6 (n = 12) or 7 to 8 (n = 16). The final form reaches distance 3 (14 to 68 percent at n = 12) and never a sparse code (0 of 12); the schedule form switches its penalty on at 0.63M to 0.91M env steps on [[12, 2, 3]] and then falls into the penalty form's distance-1 trap (0 of 12); at [[16, 4, 3]] all-to-all no form reaches distance 3 in the budget. Pricing the excess at 0.5 or 1 unit per error instead of 0.25 costs distance and buys no w*. So the constraint above n = 9 is half fixed: the distance-1 trap is gone and the bound is reachable, but the sparsity part is not yet a property of the trained policy.

experiments.ldpc_sparsity takes the sparsity part further (experiments/ldpc_sparsity/REPORT.md, runs in experiments/ldpc_sparsity/runs/; the 12-qubit cells, [[16, 4, 3]] pending): a dense per-step term in reward units (LdpcObjective(form="shaped", shaping=c), c = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2) traps at distance 1 like the penalty form; a count-unit terminal signal (form="terminal": any candidate ends the episode with 1 - h / (n - k), h the heavy generators of the sparsest basis, ldpc.heavy_generator_count) is learned fast but optimizes h rather than w* and collapses onto one dense code; the action mask ldpc.greedy_action_mask (two-qubit gates whose resulting greedy w* bound exceeds w_max are masked out of the logits) makes every terminal state feasible by construction and, on all_to_all:12, still learns distance 3 as the policy's typical output on three seeds (68 to 91 percent of terminal states at distance 3 over the last 25 updates, 769 to 2,248 distinct feasible codes per run) while trapping at w* = 4, distance 1 on square:3x4; the mask on top of the terminal reward (mask_terminal, seed 0) does it on both cells (95 and 98 percent at distance 3, all at w* = 4). The mask costs 1.3 to 2 times the wall time per env step. The default form is unchanged. On the all-to-all graph at n = 16 and 20 (--device cuda, batch 1024, 3M env steps) the same variant never reaches distance 3 (the report's scaling section), and on square:4x4 at batch 256 neither: the greedy bound over-masks as n grows (36 to 63 percent of the two-qubit actions at the end). The exact feasibility test in the mask (greedy_action_mask(method="exact"), --mask-method exact; the greedy bound as a pre-filter, then the exact rank test on the pairs it rejects, n - k <= 15) does not change that at n = 16 in 3M env steps on three seeds per graph: on all_to_all:16 it admits 4 to 7 percent of the rejected moves (the greedy bound was nearly exact) and the policy reaches one feasible [[16, 4, 3]] in 9M env steps; on square:4x4 it admits 12 to 30 percent and every run ends at distance 1. The mask costs 0.6 s per env step on the all-to-all cell (27 percent of the wall time) and 0.08 s on the lattice (the report's "Exact feasibility mask" section).

docs.title: Memory objective: design note
docs.text: Module src/autoqec_sim/memory_objective.py; experiment src/autoqec_sim/experiments/memory_objective.py; results experiments/memory_objective/REPORT.md (every number below is copied from there, which regenerates from experiments/memory_objective/runs/*.json).

docs.title: Why
docs.text: The circuit-level reward of circuit_noise scores the encoding circuit: every single fault of the noisy encoder is propagated to the output and tested with the Knill-Laflamme 1 kernel. A Hadamard on a data qubit at the end of the encoder relabels the weight-1 faults of the last layer, all of which the code detects, so the objective cannot distinguish a code from its local-Clifford deformations (the rotated surface code, XZZX 2, and the outer-column deformation tie exactly in experiments/noise_aware/runs/REPORT.md, verdict items 3, 4, and 6). Bias tailoring is a statement about how the code's stabilizers align with the dominant fault type during repeated syndrome extraction, so the reward has to be a memory experiment.

docs.title: What the objective computes
docs.text:
Input: a StabilizerCode (stabilizer generators, logical operators; CSS or not), a autoqec_sim.noise.Profile with its timing model, a scale, a number of rounds R (default the target distance), a layout, and a tier.

  1. Circuit (build_memory_circuit). One ancilla per generator, prepared in |+>, controlled-X, -Y, or -Z from the ancilla onto each support qubit in a chosen order, H, measurement in the Z basis. Generators that share a qubit with different Pauli letters cannot be interleaved (their controlled gates on that qubit do not commute), so the generators are greedily colored into batches of mutually interleavable generators (for a CSS code: the X block and the Z block) which run one after the other with their own reset and measurement layers; inside a batch the gates are packed into layers as soon as possible with one gate per qubit per layer. Preparation and final readout are noiseless MPP measurements of every generator and of the logical operators of the memory basis (Z or X); detectors compare consecutive measurements of each generator (round 0 against the preparation, the final readout against the last round), the observables compare the initial and final logical readout. Both bases are evaluated and the per-round failure probabilities are summed. The noiseless circuit has deterministic detectors for every code (test).
  2. Gate order (hook_orders, default). An X fault on the ancilla after gate t lands on the data as the product of the remaining letters of the generator (the hook). For each generator the permutations of the support are enumerated (sampled above weight 6) and the first is taken whose every proper suffix S satisfies 1 + cost(S) >= R and every contiguous segment (two ancilla faults) 2 + cost(S) >= R, with cost(S) the fewest extra single-qubit Paulis that complete S to an undetected nontrivial logical (exact, from the Knill-Laflamme kernel, cached per Pauli). This is the criterion of the ion-search schedule search. Without it the naive sorted order gives the Shor code a circuit-level distance of 1 in the Z basis (the hook of the weight-6 check is a logical operator) and the rotated surface code 2 in the X basis; with it both are 3. The order is a property of the code and is shared by the two bases.
  3. Flags (flags="one"). Each generator of weight at least three gets a flag qubit in |0> with a CNOT from the ancilla after the first data gate and another before the last, measured and declared a detector (Chao-Reichardt). Lifts the bare-ancilla d_circ of the [[5,1,3]] code from 2 to 3 (test). Needs all-to-all connectivity in this layout.
  4. Layout. all_to_all (the ion chain: ancilla j on qubit n + j) or square:RxC (data on the lattice, ancilla sites at every plaquette center including the boundary ring, edges only between a site and its corner data qubits, the rotated-surface hardware layout). Generators take sites by a greedy minimum of the path lengths to their support; a controlled gate to a non-adjacent qubit is routed along a shortest path with the nearest-neighbour CNOT ladder of the noise-aware baselines (intermediate qubits restored), and a routed generator runs in a batch of its own. The rotated surface code and XZZX route nothing; the Shor code and the discovered non-CSS 3x3 code pay in gates and depth. The profile's graph is replaced by the layout's graph, so autoqec_sim.noise.apply checks the routed circuit.
  5. Noise and DEM. The body (the R rounds) goes through autoqec_sim.noise.apply with the profile's timing (sequential for the ion presets: every two-qubit gate its own slot, idle noise on every other qubit), n_data = n for the board recipe; stim's 3 detector error model (autoqec_sim.noise.dem, loops flattened, no decomposition) gives M mechanisms with detector and observable signatures.
  6. Tiers.
  7. proxy: pfail_low_weight, the failure probability of the maximum-likelihood decoder restricted to fault sets of weight at most two: singles and pairs are grouped by syndrome, the decoder takes the observable pattern of largest summed weight per syndrome (no flip for the zero syndrome), everything else fails. Weight of a set: prod p_i (the low-p asymptote; the exclusive=True form uses the exact probability prod p_i prod (1 - p_j) and is used in the test against the exact decoder). O(M^2). Plus exact_dcirc: the exact circuit-level distance up to weight 4 with the count and summed probability product of the minimum-weight undetectable logical fault sets (ported from ion-search/lib.py; signatures wider than 64 detectors go through integer ids). Weight-3 sets are added when the number of triples is small (proxy_max_weight=3).
  8. sampled: when D + O <= 20 (detectors plus observables) the exact maximum-likelihood decoder by dynamic program over the joint (syndrome, observable) distribution, whose failure probability is exact without shots (exact_ml_failure; the construction of ion-search/decoder/exact_decoder.py); otherwise a lookup decoder built from the same weight-<= 2 fault sets with a one-mechanism completion for unseen syndromes, sampled from the DEM with distinct syndromes decoded once.
  9. bposd: the board's pinned BP+OSD decoder 45 (ldpc, minimum-sum, 30 iterations, scaling 0.625, OSD-CS order 10 clamped to the redundancy), sampled; validation only, optional dependency (uv run --with ldpc).
  10. Per-round rate: p_round = 1 - (1 - p_shot)^(1/R) per basis, summed over the two bases. MemoryResult carries the per-basis dictionaries (mechanisms, detectors, gates, layers, batches, expected faults per shot, d_circ, decoder, shots) and the summary.

docs.title: Reward
docs.text: MemoryReward(objective, d*, weight=0.1, p_ref=1e-2, clip=3): r = min(d, d*)/d* - 1 - q_1 on every state (the distance and padding terms of the noise-aware experiment) and, on states at the target distance with no weight-1 stabilizer, + weight * clip(log10(p_ref / p_round)); such a state ends the episode (the reward exposes success_fn, which CodeDiscoveryEnv adopts when none is given). A tenfold better memory rate is worth 0.1, a third of one distance quantum at d* = 3, so the term orders target-distance codes without competing with distance. Results are cached by the reduced row echelon form of the stabilizer group, so each distinct code is evaluated once per run. The term depends only on the code, not on the encoding circuit that produced it, which is the point: the encoder objective rewarded degenerate codes with weight-2 stabilizers and saturated at about ten undetected mechanisms (experiments/ion_chain/runs/REPORT.md).

docs.title: Regime of validity and scales
docs.text: The proxy is a leading-order expansion and the sampled tiers saturate once the expected number of faults per shot passes about one. At scale 1 the chain preset gives 0.6 to 3.4 expected faults per shot on the benchmark circuits, the Heron preset 2.8 to 8.8 (reset and readout flips at 1.5e-2 and a 3.5 us readout layer against T2 = 120 us, 1.5 percent dephasing per idle data qubit per readout layer), the board recipe 0.5 to 2.1. In the saturated regime the proxy is meaningless (the non-CSS 3x3 code under Heron at scale 1 on the lattice: proxy 1.8e-4, bposd 0.49) and bposd fails on a third to a half of the shots. The experiment therefore evaluates the chain preset at scale 0.25 (the labeled point of the large-code ion study), the board recipe at 1 (its canonical p = 1e-3), Heron at 0.1, and the biased-idle sweep at every rate 2.5e-4. MemoryResult reports the expected fault count per shot so a caller can see when a code is outside the regime.

docs.title: Benchmark and rank correlation
docs.text:
Benchmark (experiments/memory_objective/runs/benchmark.json): five codes ([[5,1,3]], Steane, rotated surface [[9,1,3]], the board's [[16,4,4]] SAT code, the non-CSS [[9,1,3]] of the noise-aware ion run), three profiles, R = d, all-to-all, bare ancillas, hook-aware order. p_round per code (proxy / sampled / bposd), with E the expected faults per shot:

code ion (chain 0.25) board (1) heron (0.1) [[5,1,3]], d_circ 2 0.0099 / 0.0086 / 0.0112 (E 0.16) 0.0255 / 0.0201 / 0.0293 (0.50) 0.0100 / 0.0086 / 0.0092 (0.34) Steane, d_circ 2 0.0040 / 0.0031 / 0.0067 (0.22) 0.0097 / 0.0088 / 0.0173 (0.45) 0.0031 / 0.0028 / 0.0100 (0.28) rotated surface, d_circ 3 0.00077 / 0.00079 / 0.00088 (0.24) 0.0077 / 0.0074 / 0.0074 (0.64) 0.0022 / 0.0021 / 0.0022 (0.36) [[16,4,4]], d_circ 2 0.0074 / 0.0091 / 0.0148 (0.85) 0.024 / 0.075 / 0.056 (2.13) 0.0054 / 0.0080 / 0.0085 (0.90) non-CSS [[9,1,3]], d_circ 2 0.0024 / 0.0022 / 0.0028 (0.27) 0.018 / 0.016 / 0.016 (0.80) 0.0063 / 0.0063 / 0.0065 (0.49)

The proxy is within 25 percent of the sampled tier (exact ML for the [[5,1,3]] code, the lookup decoder otherwise) on every code below one expected fault per shot, and the two rank the codes the same way on every profile (Spearman 0.9 on five codes; the [[5,1,3]] and Steane rows are within 1.15x of each other under Heron and swap). bposd deviates in two places: Steane, where it is 1.7 to 3.2 times worse than the ML tiers on every profile (the degenerate Steane DEM is a known weak case for BP), and the [[16,4,4]] code under the ion preset (2x). The [[16,4,4]] row under the board recipe (E = 2.1) is outside the regime: the lookup decoder sees mostly unseen syndromes and the proxy underestimates bposd by 2.3x. With bare ancillas every code but the rotated surface has d_circ = 2 (hook errors of the weight-4 and weight-6 checks), so the benchmark ranks codes mostly by the count and mass of their weight-2 failures, which the proxy computes exactly.

Random codes (random.json): 32 distinct [[9,1,3]] codes with no weight-1 stabilizer from random 150-gate H, S, CNOT circuits on 9 qubits (512 circuits drawn; none CSS), R = 3, all-to-all, proxy against bposd (5000 shots grown to 100 failures or 50k shots). Spearman proxy against bposd: 0.79 (ion), 0.90 (board), 0.78 (heron). All 32 have d_circ = 2 in both bases with bare ancillas, so d_circ alone does not rank them (correlation undefined); the ranking is entirely in the weight-2 failure mass. To see where the disagreement comes from (random_check.json, the same codes under the sampled lookup tier and under bposd with a second sampling seed, 100 failures per basis): proxy against sampled 0.90 / 0.81 / 0.70 (ion / board / heron), sampled against bposd 0.67 / 0.83 / 0.70, and bposd seed against seed 0.53 / 0.95 / 0.88. On the ion profile a single 100-failure bposd sample ranks the codes less consistently with a second sample than the proxy does with either, so the 0.79 is a shot-noise ceiling, not a proxy error; on board and heron the proxy against the two-seed bposd mean is 0.90 and 0.74. Two caveats. The random codes are dense (generator weights 3 to 9), so at the profile scales their expected fault counts are 0.5 (ion), 1.8 to 2.5 (board), 0.9 to 1.2 (heron): the board and heron random sets sit at the edge of or outside the leading-order regime, and the proxy's absolute values are 1.2 times the sampled tier on ion, equal on board, and 0.8 on heron (medians). The per-round rates within a profile span a factor of 2.5, so rank correlations of about 0.9 are what estimates with 10 percent relative error allow. At 400 failures per basis on the ion profile (random_check_ion400.json) the picture sharpens: proxy against sampled 0.93, sampled against bposd 0.70, bposd seed against seed 0.58 (the original 100-failure sample against a 400-failure one; their per-code ratios range from 0.77 to 1.35 while the 32 rates span 0.010 to 0.020), proxy against the two-seed bposd mean 0.69. The two maximum-likelihood estimates agree with each other on the ranking and bposd agrees with neither better than it agrees with itself, so the proxy meets the "ranks the codes the same way as tier (c)" test up to the resolution tier (c) has on this set. The lookup decoder fell back to the one-mechanism completion on 10 percent of the distinct syndromes; its absolute values are 1.19 times the proxy's (median).

docs.title: Bias sensitivity
docs.text:
Rotated surface against XZZX at n = 9, R = 3, all-to-all, bare ancillas (bias.json). The synthetic profile has every gate, reset, and measurement at 2.5e-4 and a slot idle channel of 2.5e-4 per layer with bias eta = pZ / (pX + pY). ratio = p_round(plain) / p_round(xzzx), above 1 means the objective prefers the XZZX deformation:

eta sequential: proxy sequential: bposd parallel: proxy parallel: bposd 0.5 (depolarizing) 1.000 1.08 1.000 1.05 2 1.21 1.23 1.21 1.18 5 1.55 1.25 1.53 1.59 10 1.80 1.89 1.75 1.84 30 2.06 1.87 1.96 2.32 100 2.20 2.28 2.06 2.95 inf (pure Z) 2.27 2.19 2.10 2.35

At eta = 0.5 the two codes tie to nine digits in the proxy (the deformation is a relabeling of a symmetric channel), which is the check that the preference is the bias and not the circuit. Absolute values under sequential timing: plain 0.00130 to 0.00172, XZZX 0.00130 to 0.00076 (proxy), 200k bposd shots per basis. Under the Forte set at 0.25 (duration idle with eta = 10, E = 0.20) the proxy prefers XZZX by 1.22 and the near-ML lookup decoder by 1.21 (0.000567 against 0.000467, 220k to 300k shots per basis); bposd does not (0.78: 0.000698 against 0.000894), so the pinned decoder fails to exploit the XZZX structure there. Under the chain set at 0.25 the codes tie (0.99 proxy, 0.98 bposd): its slot idle is 1e-5 per gate slot at this scale while its readout flips 2.25e-3 per ancilla dominate, consistent with the ion-search finding that the chain set makes measurement error dominant. The encoder objective could not separate the two codes under any profile (exact tie, experiments/noise_aware/runs/REPORT.md item 4).

docs.title: PPO regression
docs.text: ppo_3x3_ion_seed0.json: CodeDiscoveryEnv(n=9, k=1, square:3x3, H and CNOT, 30 gates, batch 256), MemoryReward(MemoryObjective(chain, scale 0.25, rounds=3, tier=proxy), d*=3, weight 0.1, p_ref 1e-2), PPOConfig defaults (flat MLP, 157,730 parameters), dense reward, no early stop, seed 0, one thread: 401k env steps, 13,313 episodes, 62 s. Distance 3 reached at 83,200 env steps (the noise-aware runs on the same setting reached it at 83k to 161k); 92 successful episodes, all distinct codes, 92 memory evaluations at 0.47 s each; final success rate 0.07 (the run is far from converged at this budget; the noise-aware runs needed 0.5M to 1M steps to approach 1). The best code is a non-CSS [[9,1,3]] with p_round 0.0016 under the objective, against 0.00077 for the rotated surface code and 0.0024 for the noise-aware ion seed-0 code. The test-suite regression (test_ppo_smoke_regression_3x3_ion_memory, R = 2, 300k steps or 240 s, stop at first success) passes. The memory-objective term does not change the exploration problem: the distance term drives the search to d = 3, the memory term only reorders target-distance codes, as in the noise-aware experiment.

docs.title: What a full run needs
docs.text: A real noise-aware PPO run with the memory objective at the 3x3 scale is the noise-aware protocol (8M env steps, 5 seeds, 3 profiles) with the memory term: 23k distinct target-distance codes per run at 0.47 s is about 3 process-hours per run on top of the 10 minutes of PPO, 45 runs about 135 process-hours, or 6 hours on 24 cores with the memory term evaluated in a process pool (the term is per code, embarrassingly parallel, and stim's DEM derivation is single-threaded). The 4x4 setting (d = 4, R = 4, about 2000 mechanisms per basis) costs 1.7 to 2.3 s per code in the proxy tier; with the equivariant policy's 350k to 400k steps to the first d = 4 state and the gpu_scale success rates, a 3M-step run evaluates a few thousand codes, about 2 process-hours per run. The PPO part runs on the GPU as in docs/gpu.md; the memory term stays on the CPU, so a pod with one A40 and 16 to 32 cores covers the 4x4 matrix (9 cells) in about 4 hours. Two things to decide before that run: the scale (0.25 for the chain set keeps E below one at n = 16; the [[16,4,4]] row has E = 0.85), and whether to train with flags (2.6 to 4.4 times lower p_round under the ion preset for every bare-d_circ-2 code, at 1.3 to 1.5 times the gates) or without, since the two objectives may prefer different codes.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
tests/test_memory_objective.py:

  • noiseless circuits of the [[5,1,3]], Steane, rotated surface, and the non-CSS 3x3 code have deterministic detectors in both bases, m (R + 1) detectors, k observables, n + m qubits;
  • batches follow commutation (Steane X block then Z block, [[5,1,3]] four singleton batches, the non-CSS code's batches share no qubit with different letters);
  • the hook-aware order lifts the Shor code's Z-basis d_circ from 1 to 3 and the rotated surface code's X-basis d_circ from 2 to 3;
  • one flag per generator lifts the [[5,1,3]] d_circ from 2 to 3 and adds one detector per flagged generator per round;
  • the square layout routes nothing for the rotated surface code, routes the Shor code with deterministic detectors, and the routed circuit passes the noise module's connectivity check; flags on the lattice are refused;
  • the proxy is within 10 to 20 percent of the exact maximum-likelihood failure probability on the [[5,1,3]] one-round DEM, the exclusive weight-2 and weight-3 sums increase toward it, and the lookup decoder's sampled rate agrees with it;
  • the objective prefers XZZX over the plain surface code under a Z-biased idle channel (eta = 30 and pure Z) and ties them under a depolarizing idle;
  • MemoryReward through CodeDiscoveryEnv.rollout: the [[5,1,3]] encoder succeeds with the memory term applied once, the idle element does not, and the environment adopts the reward's success_fn;
  • PPO smoke regression: 3x3 lattice, H and CNOT, chain profile at 0.25, R = 2, batch 256, 300k env steps or 240 s, must reach a verified distance-3 code (skipped without torch).

  1. Emanuel Knill and Raymond Laflamme. Theory of quantum error-correcting codes. Physical Review A, 55:900–911, 1997. arXiv:quant-ph/9604034, doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.55.900. ↩

  2. J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides, David K. Tuckett, Stephen D. Bartlett, Steven T. Flammia, and Benjamin J. Brown. The XZZX surface code. Nature Communications, 12:2172, 2021. arXiv:2009.07851, doi:10.1038/s41467-021-22274-1. ↩

  3. Craig Gidney. Stim: A fast stabilizer circuit simulator. Quantum, 5:497, 2021. arXiv:2103.02202, doi:10.22331/q-2021-07-06-497. ↩

  4. Joschka Roffe, David R. White, Simon Burton, and Earl T. Campbell. Decoding across the quantum LDPC code landscape. Physical Review Research, 2:043423, 2020. arXiv:2005.07016, doi:10.1103/PhysRevResearch.2.043423. ↩

  5. Pavel Panteleev and Gleb Kalachev. Degenerate quantum LDPC codes with good finite length performance. Quantum, 5:585, 2021. arXiv:1904.02703, doi:10.22331/q-2021-11-22-585. ↩

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Module Contents autoqec_sim.tableau Batched Aaronson-Gottesman tableau 1, one dense uint8 array of shape (batch, 2n, 2n+1). Gates H, S, S_DAG, CNOT, CZ, SWAP, and Pauli frames X, Y, Z, each applied to selected batch elements with per-element qubit indices through gather/scatter indexing (no Python loop over the batch). ActionTable resolves a vector of discrete actions with one pass per gate type. Conversion to and from stim.Tableau 2 for cross-checks. autoqec_sim.symplectic GF(2) elimination, kernel, solve; symplectic product as a float32 GEMM plus parity; logical-operator extraction by symplectic Gram-Schmidt 3 on N(S)/S; completion of a stabilizer set to a full tableau. autoqec_sim.errors Enumeration of all Paulis up to a weight, probability weighting under per-qubit Pauli channels, top-M dominant errors. autoqec_sim.reward Knill-Laflamme 4 reward of 5, r = -sum_mu lam_mu K_mu, vectorized over the batch and chunked over the error set. Detection is decided from the n+k code rows of the tableau: an error is undetected iff it commutes with every stabilizer and anticommutes with some logical (degenerate errors in S count as detected, no linear algebra needed). Also a batched exact-distance reward, a low-weight-stabilizer penalty (excludes codes padded with idle qubits), and a composite reward. autoqec_sim.code StabilizerCode read off an encoding tableau or built from Pauli strings (general non-CSS, symplectic form). Exact distance for n <= 20 by enumerating N(S) or low-weight Paulis, whichever is cheaper; randomized information-set upper bound with a witness for larger n (the symplectic version of research/kit/surrogate.py in 6); CSS test 78; weight enumerators of S and N(S). autoqec_sim.known_codes [[5,1,3]] 910, Steane [[7,1,3]] 8, Shor [[9,1,3]] 11, rotated surface 12 [[9,1,3]] and [[16,1,4]] (rotated_surface(d) builds any distance), [[4,2,2]]. autoqec_sim.graphs all-to-all, linear chain, square, triangular, heavy-hex 13 builders and a kind:size spec parser. Every builder delegates to autoqec_sim.noise.topology; from_topology, Graph.to_topology, and as_graph convert between the environment view (n, sorted edge tuple) and the noise module's graph, so the action space and the noise profile's placement check share one edge set. autoqec_sim.ldpc LDPC sparsity of a stabilizer group, batched: exact minimum bottleneck generator weight w* and a sparsest basis with its maximum qubit degree (bit-packed GF(2) elimination over the enumerated group, n - k <= 14), greedy fallback for larger codes, feasibility test ldpc_feasible, reward penalty ldpc_penalty, per-action mask greedy_action_mask (greedy bound, or the exact feasibility test after every two-qubit gate for n - k <= 15). LdpcObjective: reward and success criterion of an LDPC-constrained [[n, k, d]] target in one of four forms (penalty, unnormalized, final, schedule), exact w* on candidate states only; see "LDPC constraint". autoqec_sim.env CodeDiscoveryEnv: gymnasium-style reset/step/observation without a gymnasium dependency. State is the batched tableau; actions are single-qubit gates on every qubit and two-qubit gates on the edges of a connectivity graph (either graph class; env.topology is the noise-module view); observation is the tableau bits, the (n-k) x 2n check matrix, or a flat vector; reward modes dense 5, delta, sparse; per-element auto-reset; rollout of fixed action sequences; optional hard LDPC constraint (ldpc_w_max, modes terminate, mask, final) and feasible_action_mask(). autoqec_sim.circuit_noise Circuit-level reward under a autoqec_sim.noise.Profile (board, ion, Heron presets and their variants), a preset name, or any stim.Circuit -> stim.Circuit callable (the placeholder depolarizing model is kept). The gate list is laid out as a TICK-layered skeleton so the profile's timing and idle model apply; every fault mechanism of the noisy circuit is propagated through the rest of the encoding circuit (one GF(2) product against the symplectic map of the circuit suffix; fault_set_reference is the stim PauliString.after version, about twenty times slower, kept as the cross-check) and scored with the Knill-Laflamme kernel; dem_undetected_mass cross-checks the result against stim's detector error model. autoqec_sim.memory_objective Multi-round memory objective: an R-round syndrome-extraction circuit for arbitrary (non-CSS) stabilizer generators with one ancilla per generator, hook-aware gate orders, commutation-respecting batches, optional one-flag ancillas, all-to-all or square-lattice layouts with routed long-range gates; the autoqec_sim.noise profile with its timing model, stim's detector error model, and three fidelity tiers for the logical error rate per round (closed-form low-weight maximum-likelihood proxy with exact d_circ, exact ML or lookup-decoder sampling, pinned BP+OSD 1415 sampling). MemoryReward is the environment reward; see docs/experiments.md and docs/memory_objective.md. autoqec_sim.search Random search and an evolutionary search over gate sequences, one batched rollout per generation. autoqec_sim.regress The rediscovery regression and the autoqec-regress CLI. autoqec_sim.backends.torch_backend Opt-in torch versions of the gate kernels, ActionTable, the symplectic product, and the parity masks (undetected_mask, in_stabilizer_mask, batched_distance, the rewards) on cpu or cuda tensors, same names and semantics as the numpy functions, bit-for-bit agreement tested. The mod-2 reduction and both commutation tests run as one in-place remainder_(2) and one matrix-vector product, without the int64 copy and the boolean reductions of the numpy path. numpy_reward_adapter plugs a torch reward into the environment. See docs/gpu.md. autoqec_sim.agents.ppo PPO 16 agent (PyTorch, CPU): clipped objective, GAE 17, shared value head, entropy bonus, action masking, over the batched environment. torch is an optional dependency (rl extra) and is imported lazily. autoqec_sim.agents.ppo_regress The rediscovery regression run with PPO instead of evolutionary search, reusing the targets, reward, replay, and verification of regress, plus the PPO-only 4x4 rotated-surface target [[16, 1, 4]] (1M env steps, full budget only). autoqec_sim.experiments.noise_aware The noise-aware discovery experiment (three noise profiles, three settings, five PPO seeds each, cross-evaluation, known-code baselines, report and figures); see docs/experiments.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.scaling The RL scaling probe: diagnosis of the 4x4 failure, one-change-at-a-time variants of the agent on [[16, 1, 4]] (curriculum, macro actions, equivariant policy, batch and entropy, episode cap), and LDPC-constrained [[n, k, 3]] targets at n = 12 to 16; see docs/experiments.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.ldpc_scaling The LDPC constraint forms above n = 9: unnormalized, final, and schedule against the regression's penalty form on [[12, 2, 3]] and [[16, 4, 3]] with w_max = 4, all-to-all and square graphs, three seeds, equivariant policy, fixed budget per run; see "LDPC constraint" and experiments/ldpc_scaling/REPORT.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.ldpc_sparsity Sparsity as a property of the trained policy: the shaped (dense per-step term in reward units), terminal (count-unit signal at any candidate), and mask (greedy w* action mask) variants against unnormalized at equal budget on [[12, 2, 3]] (all-to-all, square:3x4) and [[16, 4, 3]] (square:4x4), measured as the fraction of at-distance terminal states inside the bound; see experiments/ldpc_sparsity/REPORT.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.ion_chain The noise-aware 4x4 protocol of gpu_scale (equivariant PPO, batch 1024, three profiles, cross-evaluation) on all-to-all connectivity at n = 16, the connectivity of an ion chain, with and without S in the gate set; the report compares the all-to-all codes under the ion profile with the 4x4 lattice cells of experiments/gpu_scale/runs/, the rotated surface code's lattice and all-to-all encoders, and the n = 16 known codes; see experiments/ion_chain/runs/REPORT.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.topologies The three-topology run matrix: the PPO agent alone on square, triangular, and heavy-hex lattices at two qubit-count tiers, one objective ([[n, 1, 3]], no idle qubit, H and CNOT on lattice edges, 50-gate cap), common metrics per cell (steps to success, exact d, w*, qubit degree, weight enumerators, Heron and board fault masses, rotated surface baseline); see docs/experiments.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.memory_objective Benchmark of the memory objective's tiers on five codes and three profiles, rank correlation on random distance-3 codes, the XZZX 18 bias-sensitivity test, the lattice-routing comparison, and the PPO smoke run with the memory reward; see experiments/memory_objective/REPORT.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.memory_ppo The noise-aware 4x4 protocol of gpu_scale with the memory objective as the noise term (R = 4 rounds, all-to-all layout, proxy tier in training) on four cells (chain 0.25 bare and one-flag, board 0.25, Heron 0.05), three seeds, and a second run without the LDPC term, with a gate-count term, the sampled tier outside the proxy's regime, and the sparsest generator basis; score re-evaluates the discovered codes, the encoder-objective 4x4 codes, and the rotated surface and XZZX codes under every profile at the proxy, sampled, and bposd tiers; see experiments/memory_ppo/REPORT.md. autoqec_sim.experiments.figstyle The one matplotlib style every figure of the package uses (6.5 in text width, standard heights, panel labels, profile colors).

Not included: Clifft integration and cuQuantum kernels.
